Introduction - December 2009 











##### **Introduction** 

- **_Investors still continue to dominate as a number of metals have made new highs despite rising stocks, still poor demand outside of China, and a temporary lull in imports by that country._** 

- **_Despite the above, the GFMS Base Metals Index (BMI) has made new highs reaching a peak of 279.3 on December 2.  The BMI averaged 267.8 in November compared to 262.8 in October and 149.45 in February, the lowest monthly average seen this year._** 

- **_Aluminium displ

ays the power of the funds more than most. Despite the pending closure of small capacity in Italy, this will be dwarfed by the commissioning of new capacity in the Middle East._** **_producers – has curbed the rise in LME inventories. There are some signs that demand is picking up._** - **_Although zinc prices have made sharp gains, fundamentals have worsened due to still weak demand. GFMS have increased our forecasts of the surplus for both 2009 and 2010._** ###### **Funding the base metal rally** There has been no major change in the key features of the market over the last month. Prices have generally moved higher irrespective of the fundamentals. The GFMS Base Metal Index (BMI) set a new high for the year of 279.3 on December 2, which is double the 139.7 low seen in February, and it stood at 278 on December 3. The LMEX currently stands at $3,214 compared to the year low of $1,620 in mid-February. - **_Copper’s run is better justified by the fundamentals. Although exchange stocks are trending higher, absolute levels remain low, particularly once demand improves._** - **_Significant gains in secondary production, particularly in China, are contributing to the current oversupply position in the lead market. This suggests the potential for a correction, but wider fundamentals still look positive._** - **_As we expected, levels of close to $20,000/ tonne are not justified by the recent weakness in the stainless steel market, so a move back to around $16,000 was not a surprise._** - **_The tight supply position – currently mainly emanating from the small-scale Indonesian_** Exchange stocks have continued to grow reflecting primarily the delay in the recovery in base metal demand growth outside of China. For some of the base metal demand indicators that we track, they are pointing to much slower year-on-year declines, and much more importantly at this stage of the demand cycle (i.e. a turning point) a slight improvement in month-on-month terms. However, we are slightly surprised by the slow acceleration in demand growth outside of China given the generally constructive economic data, which is largely suggesting a recovery from a low base and the fact that downstream inventories are low. ###### **China import lull should soon come to an end** Our latest research trip to China has left us fairly upbeat about demand prospects on a number of fronts. Certainly most companies are confident about the economic prospects and do not expect any bubbles to derail the robust economic growth (See page E1 for a discussion of the latest Chinese Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices

Our conversations certainly suggest that the double-digit rates of semis growth will remain a feature of the market next year. ###### **Market outlook** 

We have amended our analysis of the supply-demand balance for the fundamentals of the nickel and zinc out to 2010 reflecting the detailed work that we undertake for our Three Year Quarterly Forecast.  For details on these reports which look out to 2012, please contact charlesdemeester@gfms.co.uk.  We have both markets in surplus next year, and have increased the estimates of the surplus.  This highlights the point that these prices levels will encourage higher output, which will largely offset the much stronger demand conditions that GFMS expects in 2010. Therefore fund support will be required to support current prices levels, and particularly for zinc the upside from the price seen in early December maybe limited.  Details of our quarterly and annual forecasts and our high and low scenarios for the metals are given in the individual sections.

Economic Indicators - November 2009 











##### **Economic Indicators** 

As we mentioned in the introduction **the OECD leading indicator** (the CLI) is increasingly supportive of base metals demand even if this has yet to filter through to underlying consumption.  The latest OECD CLI for September passed 100 for the first time in 2 years.  Encouragingly the information for Europe was sharply higher at 102.7, which was the second month in a row that the index was above 100. 

The OECD CLI for **Europe** is in line with the improvement in the Eurozone Economic Sentiment index, which rose to its highest level in 14 months in November to 88.8, up from 86.1 in October.  Confidence among businesses is improving more quickly than the household sector, where concerns remain about employment and debt.  Businesses are more direct beneficiaries of the various fiscal packages. 

We also mentioned our fairly bullish views on **China** following a recent trip.  Again the latest data is positive for the base metals sector.  Chinese Industrial production was 16.1% higher year-on-year in October, driven in part by the 78.6% year-on-year surge in automobile production, while urban fixed asset investment was running 33.7% above the corresponding period of last year over the January to October period. 

The third quarter **Indian** GDP figure was upbeat rising to 7.9 % year-on-year from 6.3% year-on-year in the previous three months.  It was boosted by strong government expenditure and higher private demand, and the economy may be reverting towards trend growth of around 9%, despite still weak external demand.

Independent - Informed - International **C1** Copper - December 2009 ###### **Market background** Copper prices enjoyed further increases over the course of November and inves

tors were once again the driving force behind these gains.  The month began with prices in the mid-$6,000s and over the first half copper fluctuated within a $200 range around that level.  Boosted but an apparent deadlock emerging between workers and management of the Spence mine in Chile, prices moved decisively in the upper $6,000s in the second half of the month, the LME official price peaking at $6,946/tonne on the 23rd, up by 151% on the trough of December 2008.  Prices have continued their uptrend above $7,000/tonne in early December, even though the aforementioned issues at Spence mine were resolved. 

Contradicting its price performance (and thus confirming our contention that investors remained in the driving seat), copper’s apparent fundamentals were once again uninspiring over the course of November.  LME inventories rose by a further 68,825 tonnes to 441,000 tonnes, bringing the yearto-date net increase to 100,450 tonnes, and growth was also recorded in other exchange inventories.  Although lagged, the latest data available on Chinese imports continues to suggest that these are declining and by implication putting apparent consumption under pressure (even though real end-use demand is probably still growing).  Elsewhere, the signs are overwhelmingly suggesting of no material recovery having commenced in the mature economies. 

###### **Spence strike ends as wage talks resume** 

Ending one of the longest strikes in South American mining history, unions and owners of Chile’s Spence copper mine agreed to resume wage negotiations on 20th November.  In addition to the return of the Spence mine, output in which will return to normal levels by January, boosting production, this development also provides some relief to fears of other similar disruptions taking place in the region.  For instance, just before the commencement of the new wage negotiations 

was announced, a Chilean mine union had threatened to halt output at other mines owned by BHP Billiton, in solidarity with Spence workers. 

Added to the developments at Spence and the successful outcome of wage negotiations between BHP and miners at Escondida in October, another potential threat to production was recently removed as workers at the Antamina operation in Peru announced a deal had been reached.  The union, that had previously voted to go on strike, reached an agreement with the owners, BHP Billiton, Xstrata, Teck and Mitsubishi, on 25th November. 

All the above can by no means guarantee that frictions will be avoided in the course of upcoming negotiations for the series of labour contracts that are set to expire over the next few months in the area (Chile-Peru), as well as elsewhere. Nevertheless, evidence of both miners and operators being prepared to compromise suggests these risks are manageable.  GFMS’ own projections are conditional on such disruptions being contained, although not altogether disappearing. 

###### **Production growth remains positive** 

With key downsi

de risks to global production removed as Escondida, Spence and Antamina labour disputes are resolved, copper mine production seems set to continue growing, albeit at a relatively slow pace. We note that WBMS production figures over the last few months to September see levels averaging above 1.3 million tonnes per month, compared to the February trough of less than 1.2 million tonnes. Rising utilisation rates as well as genuine capacity growth have both contributed to this trend. This saw global production over the first nine months of the year increase by more than 2% according to the WBMS, despite losses suffered due to technical difficulties, labour-related disruptions as well as, at the margin, price related cutbacks early in the year. **C2** Independent - Informed - International Copper - December 2009 The latest relevant news releases suggest that positive growth rates, at least on a year-on-year basis, have been maintained through to the present time. In Chile, official statistics indicate copper mine production was up nearly 10% year-on-year in October, at 496,217 tonnes, even though year-to-date output was virtually unchanged. In Zambia, for which WBMS data for the third quarter seems to be estimated rather than actual, First Quantum Minerals announced that production and the Kansanshi operation in the third quarter was up by 15% year-on-year to 61,300 tonnes. ###### **Chinese imports continue to fall but stocks may be reaching ‘equilibrium’ levels** After a surprising increase in September, Chinese refined copper imports returned to their downward trajectory in October, falling by 45% month-on-month to just over 150,000 tonnes. This prompted an 18% fall in apparent consumption compared to September. Looking at semis production data, October was only marginally lower than September. On a year-on-year basis, October was the first month this year yet when the growth in semis production exceeded that in apparent consumption. Considering the outlook for copper mining, capacity expansion plans as well as efforts to improve utilisation continue, as prices float at levels close to twice their estimated average marginal production cost. The latest major announcement on this front was Chile’s Codelco nearing completion of one of the world’s largest conveyor belts, connecting its Chuquimata and Radomiro Tomic mines and boosting combined production capacity by 160,000 tonnes per year. ###### **Demand conditions yet to improve in mature economies** Against the backdrop of growing p

roduction, we have yet to see evidence of consumption recovery outside China. Despite global economic indicators being positive for a number of months, the latest WBMS release suggests that demand excluding China over the few months to September, averaging in the mid-900,000 tonnes, was still significantly lower than the norm over the last few years. Consumption in Europe has been particularly disappointing, even failing to post noteworthy month-on-month gains recently. In Japan, although the country’s Copper and Brass Association said that rolled copper products output rose for the seventh consecutive month in October, the 67,927 tonne figure was still down a hefty 12.4% year-on-year. The mismatch between the trends in real - proxied by semis production - and apparent consumption noted in October (as well as also in August) is the mirror image of the situation earlier this year, when apparent consumption growth was faster than semis output growth. During that time, although we had acknowledged that this ‘paradox’ related in part relate to lower scrap availability as well as SRB purchases, GFMS had argued that much of the ‘excess’ material had found its way into unreported inventories. In contrast, the recent reversal of conditions will almost certainly have seen the aforementioned unreported inventories decline. This would have been augmented by the persistently tight scrap market. We note that scrap imports into China fell by 36% month-on-month in October to their lowest level since February. An interesting question, at this point, is how long the stock depletion will last. Two key factors will affect this, assuming ‘real’ demand keeps to levels similar to those the last eight months of semis production data point to: the net increase in unreported inventories that took place since the final quarter of 2008 and the ‘equilibrium’ level of unreported inventories for the Chinese market. Independent - Informed - International **C3** Copper - December 2009 Starting with the latter, GFMS believe that this ‘equilibrium’ level will most probably be higher than the norm in previous years. On the one hand this is due to the growth of ‘real’ consumption and by implication its work-inprogress inventory requirements. On the other, it is due to the fact that some of the stocks are owned by private investors, serve speculative or diversification purposes and by implication are likely to prove relatively inert. The implication

ted recovery in consumption outside China to-date has been limited and more material gains now seem set to kick in well into 2010. In regards to China, the market may have to absorb news of lower imports in November and December; however GFMS expects that the strength of imports will return in early 2010. Against this backdrop, fears of supply disruptions are easing, as key potential disputes have now been resolved. Finally, as publicly available data and anecdotal information alike suggest that speculative positions are at historical highs, the risks for liquidations taking place seem significant. Independent - Informed - International **N1** Nickel & Cobalt - December 2009 ###### **Market background** Nickel prices continued their downward trend that commenced in late October touching just over a four month low to below $16,000/tonne in early December. The cash price fell by a notable $650 in the space of one day, which resulted from problems in equity markets. Prices remain subject to further weakness, however as demand for stainless steel continues to dwindle. Inventories on the LME, as a result, have continued to climb and are only 8,500 tonnes off from the historical high of 151,254 tonnes hit in November 1994. In our view, this upward trend will continue into the New Year as we not only await a demand-side recovery, but additionally the market will have to absorb higher production from the 60,000 tonnes per year Goro project and from China’s nickel pig iron producers. A more recent threat for prices however, is the potential for China’s privately held stocks to be released before the end of the year, some of which is expected to end up in LME warehouses. ###### **China remains the key demand driver** According to the World Bureau of Metals Statistics (WBMS), global nickel demand registered positive growth in September, which combined with previous monthly gains saw the year-to-date total decline by just 0.3% year-onyear. Of course this decline represents a vast improvement in comparison to the year-to-date falls noted in previous months, but notably it has solely been driven by China. Consumption elsewhere has remained lacklustre, or arguably has worsened after looking at their individual stainless markets. The WBMS estimates that China accounted for 44% of global demand in the first nine months of the year in comparison to almost half of that in the year-earlier period. Importantly, the country saw its (apparent) consumption of nickel grow by some 89% year-on-year, largely the result of its excessive importing earlier in the year. Real consumption however is much lower, as can be deduced with Antaike’s latest forecast of growth of 37.6% this year. The projection is based on 32% growth in stainless steel production, which the organisation believes will reach 9.7 million tonnes by the end of this year. Furthermore, 46% of this total will be accounted for by the 300-series, 30% from the 200-series and 24% from 400 grades of stainless steel. Looking ahead, Antaike estimates real nick

el demand growth will slow dramatically to just 5.1% in 2010 to reach 470,000 tonnes. ###### **Weak stainless demand will continue seeing prices lower** As noted in our previous monthly report, stainless mills in China curbed output in response to the huge inventory that had been built up. While the effect of these cutbacks has seen Chinese prices rise temporarily, GFMS have doubts about the sustainability of this improvement. Not only is stainless steel demand weak but reportedly many mills remain with more than sufficient stock. As a result, prices of East Asian-origin 304 stainless cold rolled sheets for December delivery have fallen to a range of RMB 17,10017,600/tonne from November’s range of RMB 17,50017,900/tonne. Recent reports suggest that Posco is likely to trim its domestic prices for December delivery after retaining its prices in November. Softer nickel prices, poor demand and rising stock levels are all behind the expected price cut. Meanwhile, production of stainless at Posco in October fell by around 3% compared with September. We believe that there is scope for lower output during the remainder of the year. Nickel Premiums Chinese Nickel Imports

**N2** Independent - Informed - International Nickel & Cobalt - December 2009 A similar situation prevails in Europe and North America. Base prices for December delivery are down on the previous month by 4.3% and 4.1%, respectively, while the alloy surcharge, based on the nickel price, in Europe is down by 2.7%, however up by almost 4.0% in North America. Outokumpu’s alloy surcharge on type 304 austenitic material is virtually unchanged at €1,005/tonne, but both austenitic 316 and ferritic 430 coil are down by about 5% month-onmonth at €1,547/tonne and €246/tonne, respectively. ###### **Global production remains low** In terms of supply, global refined production up to September fell by the same level as in the first eight months, notably 3.4% year-on-year. The Americas continued to register the steepest decline on lower output in Canada, which has been due to the strike at Vale. The only region that saw growth however was Asia. Within this, China experienced growth of 39.1% year-on-year, which indeed takes into account higher nickel pig iron production. More recent data by the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNI-A), suggests Chinese refined production at 132,000 tonnes up to October was up by almost 25% yearon-year. It should be noted that this figure does not take into account nickel pig iron production, however is primarily because of higher output at Jinchuan. The company has been maintaining output between

10-12,000 tonnes per month since the start of the year. However, there is some evidence emerging that growth in Chinese nickel pig iron production. It has been reported that some of these producers have paused their production for over a month because of the falling nickel prices. More importantly, China’s imports of nickel ore and concentrates, which have increased sharply in recent months, fell by 51.8% on September. However, it is understood that this could largely be due to the monsoon season that lies ahead in Southeast Asia (where the ore and concentrate comes from), which means mining and transporting the material becomes difficult. ###### **Chinese imports halve in October** Chinese imports of refined nickel continued the downward trend that started following the record high in July. The CNI-A estimates imports fell by almost 50% month-onmonth in October to 11,300 tonnes as higher LME prices in comparison to the domestic price made it less profitable to import. Nevertheless, year-to-date imports remained robust compared to the year-earlier period. Going forward, with the nickel price looking as if it will fall further, we expect Chinese imports to pick up in the coming months as investors will look to take advantage of the arbitrage. In contrast, exports in the country soared to 5,900 tonnes in October increasing by 86.3% on September as the price gap between the two exchanges widened. ###### **Nickel projects have been delayed** While the 60,000 tonnes per year Goro project is set to come online, there are now a few projects that have been delayed. Zambia’s 10,000 tonnes per year Munali mine will delay restarting production to early 2010 from October this year due to negotiations over working capital with a Chinese bank. It is expected the concentrate will be supplied to China’s Jinchuan. Similarly, production from the 31,000 tonnes per year Ramu nickel mine in PNG will be delayed until June 2010, which was previously expected to commence at the start of next year. We have factored in a smaller disruption allowance for 2009 as op

posed to a larger one previously, and assumed slightly higher production, while little has changed in the way we view the demand-side of the market.  We are projecting a surplus of 58,000 tonnes this year. 

Moving forward, the first half of 2010 sees the uninspiring fundamentals persist, as stainless mills adjust production to what now is a less than stellar recovery in demand for stainless products and also due to the restocking seen earlier this year and to some extent through to the present time, running out of steam. Surpluses are seen in both the first and second quarters of the year; although towards the end 

of it we expect the market will be close to balance. A swing to deficit - albeit small in magnitude - is forecast for the third and fourth part of the year, as stainless production in mature markets reclaims part of its previous losses compounding ongoing growth in developing economies. Help is also provided by the fact that output growth fails to grow as fast as planned, given the uncertainty concerning the next generation of HPAL projects and delays at some new capacities. Overall, a surplus of 23,000 tonnes is forecast for 2010. 

In terms of prices, the worsening of the market’s fundamentals in the first quarter will see prices test lower levels than during this quarter, although ongoing investor interest will, in our view, rule out a return to levels near those recorded in the aftermath of the crisis, as well as fuel short-lived ventures to the $20,000/tonne mark. Meanwhile, the commissioning of the Ramu nickel-cobalt project is on track for next month, despite previous concerns over delays. As well as the response to low prices, some unforeseen disturbances, such as the crackdown on cobalt mining activities in Congo, also served to limit metal production particularly in China. After seeing a slight deficit in 2009, we expect the market to remain in deficit in 2010 as a sharp rebound in demand outweighs the supply of metal to the market. The market will however have to absorb a number of additions to production, including the commissioning of Goro, and a number of other large scale proje

cts further down the line. However, similarly to many of the other non-ferrous metals, an improving physical balance may not necessarily see significant advances on current inflated prices. For 2010 as a whole, we forecast an average price for 99.8% of $24/lb. As demand recovers through the year, GFMS forecast a quarterly peak of around $29/lb to be reached in the third quarter. However, the aforementioned increases in production will eventually weigh on the market and we expect that prices will slip back below $20/lb by year end. In terms of alternative scenarios, we believe that there is greater upside than downside from current levels. The introduction of trading on the LME should provide a boost given the influence of funds elsewhere in base metals sector. Also there are big question marks concerning the timing about the new projects that are coming onstream, both the HPAL projects and those in the African cobalt-belt. Under high case scenario, prices could average $30/lb in the final quarter of 2010. The downside should be fairly limited given that stocks are currently low.
